title: Arendt’s Banality of Evil — thoughtlessness and responsibility
when: Developed in the early 1960s, especially through Arendt’s reporting on Adolf Eichmann’s 1961 Jerusalem trial; her book appeared in 1963. The phrase is often simplified, and its interpretation remains contested.
people: Hannah Arendt; Adolf Eichmann as the subject of her analysis; Immanuel Kant as an important background to Arendt’s later thinking about judgment.
origin: A twentieth-century European political-philosophical response to Nazi crimes, articulated by German-Jewish thinker Hannah Arendt after she emigrated to the United States.
idea: Arendt’s provocative phrase did not mean that Nazi crimes were ordinary or minor. She used “banality” to describe what she saw as the chilling shallowness and cliché-ridden thought of Eichmann, whose bureaucratic role helped enable mass murder. Her concern was that grave wrongdoing need not arise only from demonic motives: people may participate in it when they stop judging what they do and refuse to consider others’ perspectives. Arendt still treated Eichmann as responsible; the concept was not an excuse. Scholars dispute how accurately her portrait captured his ideology and motives, so it is best read as a warning and interpretive claim, not a settled psychological diagnosis.
relevance: The idea presses us to examine how routine procedures, obedience, euphemism, and fragmented responsibility can normalize harm. In institutions and automated systems alike, asking who is affected—and who remains answerable—matters as much as whether each step follows protocol.
